ft.tp.foot: If anything written here does not match reality, that is a problem to fix, not a detail.
ft.tp.intro: DARA' does not guess. Every result comes out of named layers, and every fact has a written source. This page says what is actually measured and what is not measured yet.
ft.tp.l_clf_what: A small model that compares the shape of the message with known scam messages and gives a supporting signal, never a decision. Its signal appears as evidence beside the rest.
ft.tp.l_honesty_what: Checks the model's answer before it reaches you: every red flag must appear literally in the text, and any number or institution without backing is dropped. An answer that does not hold its shape comes back as an error, not as a result.
ft.tp.l_jordan_what: Compares what arrived against the official institution directory, the campaigns documented in Jordan, DARA's own reports, and the domain registry. A lookup that did not answer shows as “could not verify” rather than counting as clean.
ft.tp.l_llm_what: Reads the message the way a person would: who it claims to be, what it asks for, where the urgency and the threat are. It runs on DARA's server, and the message text passes through it only while the check runs.
ft.tp.l_url_what: Takes the link apart and compares the part that decides where a tap goes, and checks whether the domain is young or imitates a known institution's name. DARA' never opens the link.
ft.tp.m_caveat: The Arabic subset is Arabic tweets from a public spam/ham dataset, because no public Jordanian SMS scam corpus exists. A further {n} synthetic Jordanian template rows were used in training only and are never scored. Every figure above comes from the held-out test split. The ham half of that set is largely news-agency posts, which is part of why the Arabic figure is high.
ft.tp.m_none_line: The lightweight classifier has not been measured on a test set yet, so there is no accuracy figure to print. Once it is measured, the numbers appear here as they were measured, with the test-set size and the date.
ft.tp.m_note: The figures are copied from the measurement file in the repository, with nothing rounded up.

ui.wip_sub: This screen is being built in the next phase.
ui2.banner.offline: No internet connection. The live check and reporting need one; campaigns, the directory and recovery are available.
ui2.jl.campaign.body: The team documents scam campaigns seen in Jordan, each with its source named. A match here means this domain appears in a campaign already documented, so what reached you is likely part of the same wave, and its steps are known and predictable.
ui2.jl.campaign.title: Documented campaign
ui2.jl.claimed_entity_mismatch.body: The message presents itself as a body whose official domain we know, and the domain it carries is not that one. The most common trick in this kind of scam is borrowing a familiar name with a look-alike domain. Comparing against the directory is the quickest way to be sure before tapping anything.
ui2.jl.claimed_entity_mismatch.title: Claimed body vs. the domain
ui2.jl.domain_age.body: The registration date comes from the public domain registry. Domains used in scam campaigns are usually registered shortly before the campaign and then abandoned, while official domains are old and stable. Age on its own is not a verdict, but it reads together with the other lines on this card.
ui2.jl.domain_age.title: Domain age
ui2.jl.official_match.body: We compared the domain in the message against the directory of official bodies the team reviewed, and it matches. That means the link belongs to the body itself, not to a domain that only looks like its name. The rest of the message is still worth reading calmly: a correct domain does not make everything in the message correct.
ui2.jl.official_match.title: Official body match
ui2.jl.operator.body: We read the start of the number to tell whether it is Jordanian and on which network, a landline, or foreign. The operator is not evidence of intent; its use is that a message claiming to come from a local body while its number is foreign deserves a pause before you reply.
ui2.jl.operator.title: Network operator
ui2.jl.reports.body: This counts reports that reached the DARA' platform about the same domain or number. It is not a national statistic and not any official body's record. A repeated report means other people met the same thing. No reports means nothing has reached us yet, and no more than that.
ui2.jl.reports.title: DARA' reports
ui2.jl.tld_risk.body: The extension is the last part of a domain. Some extensions are handed out cheaply and with little checking, so scam campaigns concentrate in them more than in others. This describes how the extension behaves in general, not a verdict on this particular domain.
ui2.jl.tld_risk.title: Extension risk
ui2.jl.urlhaus.body: URLhaus is a public database where security researchers share links seen distributing malware. Being listed on it is a strong signal. Not being listed does not mean safe: the database knows only what has been reported to it, and a new campaign may not have reached it yet.
ui2.jl.urlhaus.title: Threat lists
